title: Database Sharding
sources: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, ch. 6 'Partitioning': for very large datasets or very high query throughput, the data is broken up into partitions (called shards in MongoDB, Elasticsearch); each piece of data belongs to exactly one partition, and partitions are spread over many nodes so the data and the query load are spread too

Google Cloud, 'What is database sharding?' (cloud.google.com/discover/what-is-database-sharding): sharding splits a large database into smaller pieces called shards, each stored on a separate server, a form of horizontal scaling; a shard key decides which shard each row goes to

MongoDB Manual, 'Ranged Sharding' and 'Shard Keys': ranged sharding divides data into contiguous ranges of shard key values; a poorly chosen shard key (low cardinality, uneven frequency, or monotonically increasing) concentrates reads/writes on one shard, a hot spot, while others sit underused
DDIA ch. 6 'Skewed workloads and relieving hot spots': if partitioning is unfair, one partition takes most of the load (a hot spot) and the others sit idle

lines.text: Yesterday we gave our database copies,
but each copy still holds every order,
and soon that's too much for one machine.
Sharding splits the data into pieces.
Think of tearing the order book by name:
A to H here, I to P there, Q to Z there.
lines.caps: A TO *H | *HERE | I TO *P | *THERE | Q TO *Z | *THERE

lines.text: Each piece is a shard, on its own machine,
so each one stores less and does less work.
To find Asha's order, look at the shard key.
Her name starts with A, so it's shard one.
The catch? Pick a bad key, and one shard gets slammed,
lines.caps: THE *CATCH | PICK A *BAD | *KEY | AND ONE *SHARD | GETS *SLAMMED

lines.text: Too big for one machine? Split it.
